articles.title: El Paso investigators detail 9 years of alleged restroom spying by 'peeping tom'
articles.description: El Paso deputies arrest alleged 'peeping tom' after gas station restroom incident EL PASO, Texas (KFOX14/CBS4) -- Police documents show more "peeping tom" allegations against the 36-year-old man who was arrested on July 2 for allegedly spying on a woman in a gas station restroom. The complaint affidavit for Ivan Abraham Ponce lists and describes in detail several instances in the past nine years where he allegedly either spied on or recorded women in public restrooms. The most recent one (and the one previously reported) happened on June 29, at around 9:36 a.m., at a Circle K gas station on 12281 Eastlake Blvd. in the Lower Valley. According to the affidavit, deputies with the El Paso County Sheriff's Office answered the call and spoke with the victim, who said she was in a stall when she heard footsteps, "a slapping noise," and heavy breathing. The victim said she got scared, feeling like someone was spying on her, and so she pulled her garments up and waited in the stall until she heard footsteps leaving the restroom. In the affidavit, deputies describe watching surveillance video from the gas station, which appears to show Ponce hanging out outside the restrooms before following a woman inside. Snippets from the surveillance video were then shared on the popular social media account @therealfitfamelpaso. WATCH: Deputies stated that they recognized Ponce, noting that he worked at the El Cometa on 9529 Viscount Blvd. in East El Paso. With the suspect identified, deputies said they ran a history check on Ponce, learning about four more incidents allegedly involving Ponce doing the same thing in other public restrooms, twice in the same restaurant. Previous incidents The affidavit alleges that on Dec. 10, 2025, and March 30, 2025, two incidents were reported at the restaurant Rudy's located at 7970 Gateway East Blvd. in the Lower Valley. Following the most recent incident at the Circle K, investigators met with some of the victims. In the affidavit, investigators describe their conversation with the manager of Rudy's. She alleges that she was inside a stall in the restroom when she spotted Ponce looking at her through the crack by the wall. "Hey, somebody is in here," the victim recalls saying before chasing after him; however, she said that by the time she stepped out, Ponce had left the restaurant. The manager also told investigators that she saved the surveillance video from that day in case Ponce ever came back, and she alleges that he did some months later and did the same thing to another woman. This time, the victim, who was 18 years old, was reportedly in the restroom recording a "TikTok" video when she saw a cellphone flash as if someone was taking photo or video of her. On Dec. 8, 2019, the affidavit alleges that Ponce went into the women's restroom at the Starr Western Wear store located at 750 Sunland Park Dr. and recorded a woman. On August 4, 2017, the affidavit alleges Ponce was cited for going into the women's restroom at 4849 N. Mesa St. and peeping into a stall. Questions It is unclear what happened in the investigations surrounding those previous incidents at Rudy's. The cases were opened by the El Paso Police Department, but according to the affidavit, investigators found that they were inactive. According to the affidavit, the investigator reached out to EPPD to adopt the case where Ponce allegedly recorded the woman inside the Rudy's restaurant. KFOX14/CBS4 reached out to EPPD to learn why the cases were inactive. And while police couldn't comment on the cases, an EPPD spokesperson told us that when a case is "inactive," it doesn't mean it's closed, but just that, for various reasons, like lack of information, the investigation has been paused. Below is EPPD's full statement: An inactive case is not a closed case, and there can be many reasons why a case is inactive. I can't tell you the exact reason for the cases you are inquiring about, however some reasons could be that the investigator has paused the investigation pending more leads, there may not be enough workable information to make an arrest, all potential investigative steps have already been explored and sometimes there is limited cooperation from complainants or witnesses. Again, this is just in general and not specifically to the cases you are inquiring about. What's next? Jail records show Ponce was booked into the El Paso County Downtown Jail on Tuesday, where he was charged with two counts of voyeurism and one count of invasive visual recording. According to jail records, Ponce remains in jail under a combined bond of $320,000. Court records show a bond hearing is scheduled for Ponce for Thursday morning. pendingReview.title: Rogue Police Officers Have Turned Flock's Nationwide Camera Network Into a Stalking Tool
pendingReview.description: A woman found her police officer ex-boyfriend cop had used Flock's camera system 600 times to look up the location of her and her daughter, reports the Washington Post (Alternate URL here). (She found out through Have I Been Flocked, described as "a website that aggregates police search logs made available through public records.") But it turns out dozens more police officers have also misused Flock... Authorities have charged or accused at least 50 law-enforcement officers of using license-plate readers for unauthorized purposes, including to stalk women without their knowledge or consent, a Post analysis of police and court records found. In 26 of these cases, police investigators and prosecutors said the officers used the technology to spy on their wives, their girlfriends, their exes, their exes' new partners or women they wanted to meet. In other cases, police or prosecutors have not specified the alleged surveillance targets. Flock's system was used in 46 of the cases analyzed by The Post, while the other cases involved competing products... After The Post relayed its findings to Flock, the company said in a statement it "will soon be announcing better filters and tools to stop abuse before it happens...." In April, the company rolled out a new voluntary "audit assistance" feature, which agencies can choose to enable, that automatically scans officers' searches for suspicious activity, such as queries repeatedly targeting the same vehicle or run by officers off the clock. In an interview with The Post, Flock chief executive Garrett Langley said misuse of its systems is inevitable and that the company is focused on providing tools to catch perpetrators after the fact... "We're not going to change humans, and humans make bad decisions," Langley said. "What we can do is make sure that they know if you use this tool, you will be held accountable...." Through automated license-plate reader systems, or ALPRs, officers could trace the rhythms and travels of their subjects' daily lives, leading in some instances to violent confrontations, moments of psychological manipulation, and threats of coercion and control, the analysis found. - In Wisconsin, a police officer allegedly used Flock to check whether his ex-girlfriend had gone to an abortion clinic, according to a police affidavit for a case set for trial this month. - In Kansas, a police chief who tracked his ex through Flock sneaked up on her while she was intimate with another man, a state police certification body alleged, leading to his firing. - In Florida, a deputy speeding to stop a young actress he'd added to a watch list for a license-plate tool called Guardian nearly caused a head-on crash, according to a police report and video from his dashboard camera. The deputy was arrested in March, and his attorney declined to comment. - And in California, prosecutors said a former deputy, Alexander Vanny, used Flock as part of a months-long campaign of "stalking" and "humiliating" his former fiancée that also involved following her around town and installing a hidden camera in her roommate's bathroom, according to a sentencing brief... While some of the searches resulted in officers' firings, prosecutions and prison sentences, police departments in other cases allowed officers to continue using the systems even after receiving warnings that they were being misused... An array of privacy advocates has argued that Flock could deter bad actors by making simple changes to its product, such as requiring officers to label every search with a criminal case number. Some policing experts also warned that agencies' inconsistencies in developing and enforcing standard procedures for license-plate readers could lead to further misconduct. With no federal laws governing use and only a patchwork of state laws, many of the country's roughly 18,000 police agencies are left to decide their rules on their own... Langley, Flock's chief, has dismissed pushes by activists for the company to further limit how officers use its product. "No one elected me the police chief of America," he told Forbes last year, adding, "I don't think it's our job to police the police." The Post also got this quote from an officer was fired and sentenced to probation after pleading no contest to charges of computer-system misuse, stalking and battery. "Pretty much everybody uses that computer system" improperly in the department, he said, and "they don't audit it [nearly] as much as they should." Flock told The Post it now has over 120,000 cameras in more than 6,000 communities, recording 20 billion license plate scans every month. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

pendingReview.title: Voyeuristic doctor's appeal against conviction fails - Jersey Evening Post
pendingReview.description: A CAMBRIDGE-EDUCATED doctor who was found guilty of secretly filming men in bathrooms has failed to overturn his conviction. Earlier this year, Jurats found Diego Balassini (28) guilty of nine counts of voyeurism and was sentenced to a two-year probation order which requires him to participate in mental health treatments. Balassini was also placed on the sex offenders register. Last week, the Court of Appeal upheld his conviction. Balassini was training as a doctor at the Hospital and had hoped to complete a doctorate at Oxford University but was suspended from practicing as a doctor in the UK following his conviction. His offending came to light when a gymgoer caught Balassini filming him in a changing room and confronted him. The gymgoer found footage of himself naked on Balassini's phone and police arrested Balassini shortly after. Videos found on his phone showed that the doctor had also filmed men urinating in two town bars and at Jersey Airport - positioning himself at the urinal and filming both himself and others in the background. Snapchat conversations and internet search terms also showed a sexual interest in urination, according to the prosecution - with search terms referring specifically to urination filmed in secret. For Balassini to be found guilty, he had to take the videos with the purpose of "obtaining sexual gratification". He argued that he suffered from complex mental health issues and had dissociated when he took the recordings. Appealing against the conviction this week, Balassini's lawyer Advocate Stephen Baker argued that an expert psychologist's evidence was dismissed too easily and that the judge had an "overall imbalance" in his interventions. Though it felt that there was "some force" in the argument, the Court of Appeal in rejecting Balassini's appeal, said: "In the circumstances of this case, there is no difficulty. The evidence as a whole showed that sexual gratification as a purpose was possible, not unlikely." This, the judgment continued, did not stop the Jurats from finding that he did do it for sexual gratification, and their conclusion was "entirely unsurprising". Advocate Baker also argued that the indictment did not mention that the offence included observing or looking at images, and that Balassini had deleted four videos without watching them. The Court of Appeal said that missing out those words "is regrettable and should not be replicated in future cases", stressing the importance of "precision" - but found that Balassini was not at a disadvantage. Jonathan Crow CVO KC was presiding, with David Perry KC and Roddy Dunlop KC.
